content: Vitis vinifera, commonly known as the common grapevine, is a species of the genus Vitis. It is native to the Mediterranean region, central Europe, and southwestern Asia, spanning from Morocco and Spain in the west to northern Iran in the east, and extending northward to southern Germany. This plant is a liana, capable of growing up to 35 meters in height, and is characterized by its flaky bark. Its leaves are alternately arranged, palmately lobed, and measure between 5 to 20 cm in both length and width. The fruit of Vitis vinifera is a berry, commonly referred to as a grape. In its wild form, the berries are approximately 6 mm in diameter, ripening to a dark purple or blackish color with a pale waxy coating. In cultivated varieties, the berries are significantly larger, reaching up to 3 cm in length, and can be green, red, or purple in color. This species is typically found in humid forests and along streamsides. The wild grape is often classified as Vitis vinifera subsp. sylvestris, while the cultivated forms are referred to as Vitis vinifera subsp. vinifera. Domesticated grapevines possess hermaphroditic flowers, whereas the wild subspecies sylvestris is dioecious, meaning male and female flowers are borne on separate plants, necessitating pollination for fruit development. Wild grapes were historically harvested by foragers and early agricultural societies. For thousands of years, the fruit has been valued for both its medicinal and nutritional properties, with its history deeply intertwined with the development of winemaking. Changes in the shape of grape seeds (narrower in domesticated forms) and their geographic distribution suggest that domestication occurred around 3500–3000 BCE in southwestern Asia or southern Transcaucasia, including present-day Armenia and Georgia. The cultivation of domesticated grapes subsequently spread to other parts of the Old World during prehistoric or early historic times. Grapes accompanied European colonists to various parts of the world, arriving in North America around the 1600s, and later spreading to Africa, South America, and Australia. In North America, Vitis vinifera hybridized with native Vitis species, some of which were intentionally bred to combat phylloxera, an insect pest that devastated European grapevines but had a lesser impact on North American species. This pest caused widespread destruction of European wine production within a few years. Subsequently, North American rootstocks were widely adopted for grafting Vitis vinifera cultivars to confer resistance to phylloxera. In North America, the cultivation of Vitis vinifera was initially limited to the relatively mild climates of the West Coast, including New Mexico, California, and the Pacific Northwest. However, due to the pioneering research of Konstantin Frank, the species is now successfully grown in harsher climates such as New York State, western Michigan, and southern Ontario. Dr. Helmut Becker's work in the early 1980s introduced Vitis vinifera to the Okanagan Valley in British Columbia. In March 2007, Australian scientists from the CSIRO, working within the Cooperative Research Centre for Viticulture, discovered that rare and independent mutations in two genes led to the emergence of a single white grapevine, which became the progenitor of nearly all white grape varieties worldwide. If only one of these genes had mutated, most grapes would still be red, and the more than 3,000 white grape cultivars available today would not exist. The use of grapes dates back to Neolithic times, as evidenced by the discovery of 7,000-year-old wine storage jars in present-day northern Iran in 1996. Additional evidence indicates that the Mesopotamians and Ancient Egyptians cultivated grapevines and possessed winemaking skills. Greek philosophers extolled the healing properties of grapes, both as whole fruits and in the form of wine. In China, the cultivation of Vitis vinifera and winemaking began during the Han Dynasty in the second century CE, following the species' introduction from Ta-Yuan. However, wild grape species such as Vitis thunbergii, known as mountain grapes, were used for winemaking prior to this period. In European folk medicine, the sap of grapevines was used to treat skin and eye diseases. Historically, grape leaves were employed to stop bleeding and alleviate the pain and inflammation associated with hemorrhoids. Unripe grapes were used to treat sore throats, while raisins were administered as remedies for tuberculosis, constipation, and thirst. Ripe grapes were utilized in the treatment of cancer, cholera, smallpox, nausea, skin and eye infections, as well as kidney and liver diseases. Although seedless grape varieties were developed to appeal to consumer preferences, researchers have discovered that many of the health benefits of grapes may actually originate from the seeds themselves. In culinary traditions, grapevine leaves are used in dishes such as the Balkan dolma, where they are stuffed with minced meat (such as lamb or beef), rice, and onions.
